name: Perilla Purple
lede: Perilla Purple is a dusty, reddish mauve named for the dark purple-red leaves of perilla, the East Asian herb better known in the kitchen as shiso.

sections.title: A leaf, not a flower
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color standards place this hue on plate XXXVII, hue 65'', tone k; it is reproduced from a scan of an aged plate, so the printed color is approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it in block 259, "grayish purplish red", and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives it a first recorded date of 1912, on plate 47 J 3 [2][3]. In Munsell it reads 8.3RP 3.7/4.0, a muted red-violet far from the flat purple most people picture when they hear "perilla" [1].

The perilla plant itself, a mint-family herb grown across East Asia, has a purple-leaved variety whose color runs darker and more saturated than this swatch [1]. The nearest named color in our data is [[dark-vinaceous-purple|Dark Vinaceous-Purple]], 2.6 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[dahlia-carmine|Dahlia Carmine]], [[dark-mauve|Dark Mauve]] and [[corinthian-purple|Corinthian Purple]] close behind [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Perilla Purple appears in 46 of our 23,781 paintings, about 0.19 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 20 of them, rarer than 61 percent of our named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 5 of 1,674 paintings, at 2.5 times the expected rate for that century [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, present in 35 percent of the 20 paintings where it carries real area [4].

The earliest match is dated 1550, in a work by Michele Tosini — 362 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name, as photographed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. In printed English, the term "perilla purple" peaked in the 1930s, after rising fastest in the 1910s [4].
